title: Deep learning quickfire
objectives: Answer short questions on initialisation, normalisation, dropout, attention scaling and the loss at the start.

screens.title: The first number printed
screens.prose: This lesson takes about fifteen minutes: ten quick questions at interview pace, one minute each. Lessons are not timed, so set your own clock. A character model predicts one of 65 characters, with small random weights and a softmax cross-entropy loss.
screens.question: What should the loss be at step 0? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: At initialisation every character is about equally likely.
The loss is $-\ln p$ of the right character, with $p = 1/65$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take minus the log of a uniform probability.

byKey.inverse: That is the probability $1/65$. The loss is minus its log.
byKey.log10: You used base 10. Cross-entropy uses the natural log.

explain.text: Near-uniform predictions give each character $1/65$, so the loss is $\ln 65 = 4.1744$. A first loss far from this means a bug before any training.

screens.title: Why divide by the root of d
screens.prose: A query and a key each have $d$ independent standard normal entries. Slide $d$ and watch the spread of their dot product, before and after dividing by $\sqrt{d}$.
screens.question: For $d = 64$, what is the standard deviation of $\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{k}$ before scaling?

hints.text: Each product $q_i k_i$ has mean 0 and variance 1.
A sum of 64 independent ones has variance 64.
The sd is $\sqrt{64} = 8$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the variances, then take the root.

byKey.var: That is the variance. The sd is its root.

explain.text: The variance adds up to $d$, so the sd is $\sqrt{d} = 8$; a simulation of 20,000 pairs gives $8.037$. Dividing by $\sqrt{64}$ brings it to $1.005$, so the softmax does not saturate as $d$ grows.

screens.title: He initialisation
screens.prose: A ReLU layer has fan-in 512. He initialisation keeps the variance of activations steady from layer to layer.
screens.question: What standard deviation do its weights get? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: He initialisation sets the variance to $2/\text{fan-in}$.
The 2 makes up for the ReLU zeroing half the inputs.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use variance $2/\text{fan-in}$, then take the root.

byKey.xavier: That is $\sqrt{1/512}$, which ignores the ReLU. He doubles the variance to make up for it.
byKey.variance: That is the variance, $2/512$. The sd is its root.

explain.text: A ReLU passes about half the variance, so He uses $2/512$, an sd of $0.0625$. The spoken sentence: variance two over fan-in, because ReLU halves it.

screens.title: Inverted dropout
screens.prose: Dropout with $p = 0.2$ zeroes each unit with probability 0.2 during training. Inverted dropout rescales the units it keeps.
screens.question: By what factor are the kept units multiplied during training?

hints.text: The expected value of a unit must not change.
A unit survives with probability 0.8.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Keep the expected value of each unit the same.

byKey.keep: That is the survival probability. Divide by it to keep the mean.
byKey.drop: You divided by the drop rate 0.2. Divide by the keep rate 0.8.

explain.text: Each unit survives with probability 0.8, so multiplying by $1/0.8 = 1.25$ keeps its mean. At test time every unit is kept and nothing is scaled.

screens.title: Two norms at test time
screens.prose: Batch norm normalises each feature over the batch. Layer norm normalises each token over its own features.
screens.question: What does each use at test time?

options.text: Batch norm: running averages. Layer norm: nothing stored.
Both use the statistics of the test batch.
options.why: Batch norm's output would then depend on which examples share the batch. It uses running averages.

options.text: Both use running averages from training.
options.why: Layer norm's statistics come from the token itself, so it computes them fresh every time.

options.text: Neither of them normalises anything at test time.
options.why: Both still normalise; only where batch norm's statistics come from changes.

hints.text: Which of the two needs other examples to compute its statistics?
Batch norm does; layer norm uses one token.
So only batch norm needs stored statistics.

feedback.correct: Running statistics for batch norm; nothing stored for layer norm.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask where each one's mean and variance come from.

byKey.batch: Then one example's prediction would depend on the others in its batch.

explain.text: Batch norm keeps running means and variances during training and uses them at test time. Layer norm computes its statistics from each token, so training and test match.

screens.title: Dropout at test time?
screens.prose: A candidate says: "At test time dropout uses the last training mask. That way the network matches what it learned."
screens.question: What is right?

options.text: Dropout is off: every unit kept, nothing rescaled.
Use the last training mask, as the candidate says.
options.why: A fixed mask throws away a fifth of the network for every prediction, for no reason.

options.text: Keep every unit and multiply by 0.8.
options.why: That is the old, non-inverted dropout. Inverted dropout already scaled during training.

options.text: Draw a fresh mask for each test example.
options.why: That makes predictions random. It is a technique for uncertainty, not the default.

hints.text: What does inverted dropout already do during training?
It divides kept units by 0.8.
So at test time nothing is dropped and nothing is scaled.

feedback.correct: Off at test time; inverted dropout needs no rescaling.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about what the training-time scaling was for.

byKey.same: A frozen mask removes a fifth of the units from every prediction.

explain.text: The training-time division by 0.8 makes each unit's mean match the full network. So at test time we keep everything and scale nothing.

screens.title: A batch of one
screens.prose: You train with batch norm, but memory forces a batch size of 1.
screens.question: What happens to a batch-norm layer during training?

options.text: In a fully connected layer every centred value is 0, so the layer outputs $\beta$.
Nothing changes: it normalises the one example as usual.
options.why: With one example the batch mean is the value itself, so every centred value is 0.

options.text: It divides by zero and returns NaN.
options.why: The $\epsilon$ in the denominator prevents that; the output is simply constant.

hints.text: Compute the mean of a batch of one value.
The value minus its mean is 0.
So the output is $\gamma \times 0 + \beta = \beta$, whatever the input.

feedback.correct: The layer outputs $\beta$ and carries no information; use layer norm.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compute a batch mean and variance with one example.

byKey.fine: With one example the centred value is exactly 0.

explain.text: With one example, $x - \mu = 0$ for every feature, so batch norm outputs $\beta$ and no gradient reaches the input through it. Layer norm or group norm does not depend on the batch.

screens.title: One sentence and its reason
screens.prose: Each quick answer is a fact and a reason, said in one breath: $$\text{loss}_0 \approx \ln V, \quad \sigma_{\text{He}} = \sqrt{2/n_{\text{in}}}, \quad \text{keep} \times \tfrac{1}{1 - p}, \quad \frac{\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{k}}{\sqrt{d}}$$
screens.question: Which answers give a correct reason? Select all that apply.

options.text: The first loss is about $\ln V$, because untrained predictions are near uniform.
Attention divides by $\sqrt{d}$, because the dot product's sd grows as $\sqrt{d}$.
He initialisation doubles the variance, because a ReLU zeroes about half its inputs.
Layer norm needs running statistics, because tokens differ in length.
options.why: Layer norm uses each token's own features and stores nothing.

options.text: Dropout scales by $1 - p$ at test time, because units were dropped in training.
options.why: Inverted dropout scales by $1/(1 - p)$ in training and does nothing at test time.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check each reason against what the method does.

explain.text: A good quick answer names the number and the cause. "Because" is the word the interviewer is waiting for.

screens.title: A code review at a lab
screens.prose: You review a colleague's run at a lab. The model has 65 output classes, and the first loss printed is 9.7.
screens.question: What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The output weights start too large: confidently wrong.
Nothing: the loss falls, so training works.
options.why: It should start near $\ln 65 = 4.1744$. It wastes steps unlearning a bad start.

options.text: The learning rate is set far too high for this model.
options.why: Step 0 is before any update, so the learning rate cannot have caused it.

options.text: The labels leak into the inputs of the model.
options.why: A leak makes the loss too low, not too high.

hints.text: What should step 0 print for 65 classes?
A higher value means large logits at the start: scale the last layer down.

feedback.correct: Large initial logits; shrink the last layer's weights.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare 9.7 with what step 0 should print.

byKey.fine: Falling is not enough: it starts more than twice too high.

explain.text: Step 0 should print about $4.1744$; 9.7 is $2.32$ times that. Large initial logits put high confidence on wrong classes, so scale the output layer down at initialisation.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: The interviewer goes on: "Your loss starts at 0.01 for 65 classes. What is wrong?"
screens.question: Select all that apply.

options.text: The labels leak into the inputs.
A causal mask is missing, so each position sees the token it must predict.
The loss is divided by the wrong count, for example by $V$ as well.
Nothing: the model is simply very good at the start.
options.why: An untrained model cannot beat uniform guessing by that much: it should start near $4.1744$.

options.text: The learning rate is too low.
options.why: Step 0 is before any update, so the rate plays no part.

hints.text: A loss of 0.01 means near-certain right answers before training.
Something lets the model see the answer, or the loss is not what it claims.
A leak, a missing mask, or a mean over the wrong axis.

feedback.correct: Each one makes the loss look far too good.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask how an untrained model could look certain.

byKey.good: An untrained model sits near uniform, about $\ln 65$.

explain.text: A starting loss far below $\ln V$ means the model can see the answer or the loss is mis-computed. Check the inputs for the target, the mask, and the reduction axis.

screens.title: The check in code
screens.prose: Write `sanity_checks(logits, targets)`. Return $\ln V$, the actual mean cross-entropy, and a flag. The flag is true when the two differ by more than half of $\ln V$. Compute the loss without overflow.
screens.question: Complete the function.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np


def sanity_checks(logits, targets):
    # logits: (batch, V); targets: (batch,) class indices
    # return (expected starting loss, actual mean cross-entropy, flag)
    # flag is True when actual differs from expected by more than half of expected
    ...
widget.solution:
import numpy as np


def sanity_checks(logits, targets):
    z = np.asarray(logits, dtype=float)
    t = np.asarray(targets)
    expected = float(np.log(z.shape[1]))
    m = z.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    lse = m[:, 0] + np.log(np.exp(z - m).sum(axis=1))
    actual = float(np.mean(lse - z[np.arange(len(t)), t]))
    flag = abs(actual - expected) > 0.5 * expected
    return expected, actual, flag
widget.how: Submit runs 6 hidden tests. Test 1 uses uniform logits over 65 classes and expects $\ln 65$ twice and no flag. Test 2 is a small hand case, test 3 a planted leak that must be flagged, test 4 a logit of 800, and test 5 the expected value for 27 classes. Test 6 has nearly uniform logits and no flag. Numbers are compared to $10^{-9}$ relative.

    actual = float(np.mean(lse - z[np.arange(len(t)), t]))
    flag = abs(actual - expected) > 0.5 * expected
    return expected, actual, flag

def sanity_checks(logits, targets):
    z = np.asarray(logits, dtype=float)
    t = np.asarray(targets)

mutants.symptom: Exponentiates without subtracting the row maximum, so a logit of 800 overflows.

hints.text: $V$ is the number of columns of `logits`.
Cross-entropy per row is $\log\sum_j e^{z_j} - z_{\text{target}}$; subtract the row maximum first.
Average over rows, then compare with $\ln V$.

feedback.correct: Uniform logits give exactly $\ln V$, and the leak is caught.
feedback.generic: Not yet. Check $V$, the log, the mean and the flag.

byKey.test-1: Uniform logits over 65 classes should give $4.1744$ for both numbers. Take $V$ from the number of columns, use the natural log, and average the rows.
byKey.test-3: A planted leak gives a tiny loss, which must be flagged too. Flag a difference either way.
byKey.test-4: A logit of 800 overflowed. Subtract each row's maximum before exponentiating.

explain.text: Two numbers and a comparison catch most broken pipelines before any training. The log-sum-exp with the maximum subtracted keeps it finite for any logits.

ideas: The first loss should be about $\ln V$: $4.1744$ for 65 classes; far above or below it means a bug.
He initialisation uses sd $\sqrt{2/n_{\text{in}}}$, $0.0625$ for fan-in 512; inverted dropout scales kept units by $1/(1 - p)$ in training only.
Batch norm uses running statistics at test time and fails with a batch of one; attention divides by $\sqrt{d}$ to keep the scores' sd near 1.
summary.trap: Dropout is off at test time; inverted dropout already scaled during training.

quiz.question: A names model predicts one of 27 characters. What should its loss be at initialisation? Give 4 decimal places.

byKey.inverse: That is the probability. The loss is minus its log.

quiz.question: Inverted dropout with $p = 0.5$: by what factor are kept units multiplied in training?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide by the keep probability.

byKey.keep: That is the keep probability. Divide by it.

explain.text: Half the units survive, so each kept unit is multiplied by 2 to keep the mean.

quiz.question: What is the He initialisation sd for a ReLU layer with fan-in 128? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Variance $2/\text{fan-in}$, then the root.

byKey.xavier: That ignores the ReLU: use 2 over fan-in.
byKey.variance: That is the variance. Take its root.

quiz.question: Query and key vectors have 16 independent standard normal entries. What is the sd of their dot product before scaling?

byKey.var: That is the variance. Take its root.

explain.text: The variance is 16, so the sd is 4, and dividing by $\sqrt{16}$ brings it to 1.
